item.passage:
The power went out at twenty past seven, in the middle of dinner, with a sound from the street like a door being shut hard. For a second the kitchen was completely dark. Then the refrigerator's hum and the furnace fan came back to Amara all at once, as things she could no longer hear.

Her father found the flashlight in the drawer by the sink. It gave a brown glow for about a minute and went out. Her mother found the candles from Amara's last birthday, which were short and striped and burned quickly, and they finished their soup by the light of a one and a four.

By eight the house had begun to cool. Ice had been falling since the afternoon, and from the window Amara could see the lines along the street sagging under it, glazed like the inside of a bottle. Her father carried an armload of wood in from the porch and lit the stove in the living room, the black iron one that had come with the house and that they had used perhaps twice. It smoked, then caught. Because it was the only warm room, everyone moved there: her parents, Amara, her brother Theo, and the cat, who took the spot nearest the fire as though she had been waiting years for it.

Theo was eight and kept forgetting. Their father had brought a second flashlight in from the car, and every time Theo carried it down the hall to the bathroom, he flipped the light switch on the way in. Every time he came back, he reported that it still wasn't working.

Amara's phone was at nineteen percent. She had an essay due in the morning, half of it saved on a laptop whose battery had died at eight, and she spent the first hour refreshing the power company's map, a scatter of red dots that did not change. Then her mother took a deck of cards from the desk and asked whether anyone remembered how to play hearts.

Nobody did, exactly. They argued the rules into existence. Her father insisted the queen of spades was worth thirteen points; Theo wanted it to be worth a hundred. They settled on thirteen, and Theo kept score anyway in a system of his own, on the back of an envelope, holding it close to the stove door to see. Somewhere in the second game Amara put her phone face down on the arm of the couch and pulled her chair in.

At a quarter to eleven the lights came on all over the house at once. The refrigerator shuddered, the furnace started, and the microwave began to flash 12:00 in green. Her father went to check the freezer. Her mother went to plug in her phone. Theo was asleep against the cat.

Amara looked at the table. The cards lay where they had been dropped, face down, a hand half played. She set Theo's envelope on top of them, squared the edges of the pile, and left it there.

All summer I kept the garden on a schedule:
beans on Mondays, squash on Thursdays,
the tomatoes every evening at six
with the green hose I dragged along the rows
like a dog that would rather stay on the porch.

I had a chart taped inside the shed door.
I had a gauge on a post, a plastic cup
with lines on it for measuring the sky's part,
which all through July was nothing.

Then on a Tuesday in August, unscheduled,
the rain came over the fence without knocking
and watered everything at once:
the beans, the squash, the bare path,
the chair I had left out, the seed packets
stuck on sticks at the ends of the rows.

Nobody had told it about the rows.
It gave the weeds exactly what it gave the lettuce,
put an inch of water in the wheelbarrow,
and more in the gauge in an hour
than the whole of July had managed.

The nasturtium leaves held it up in beads
and tipped it off like coins from a tray.
The dust on the squash leaves ran to mud
and the mud ran off. A snail
came out on the walk to take the air,
the first I had seen since June.

I stood in the doorway of the shed
with the nozzle of the coiled hose in my hand
as if it might still be wanted.
Then I set it down and walked out
without a hat, and got as wet
as the tomatoes, which by then

looked, I have to say, much better
than they ever had at six o'clock.

The winter I was eleven, I jumped from the top of the playground slide on a dare and broke both bones in my lower left leg. Setting them took an operation and two metal pins, and I spent four nights in the children's ward of the county hospital, in a room with two beds.

The other bed, the one by the window, belonged to a girl named Dana. She was fourteen and had been there, she told me, since before Halloween. It was the second week of December. She had a stack of library books on her tray table, a paper chain taped along the bed rail, and the manner of someone who had watched a good many eleven-year-olds with broken legs come and go.

My first night, the machine beside my bed began to beep, and I pressed the call button five times. Dana told me from the dark that it was the pump, that it beeped when the bag of fluid ran low and for no other reason, and that the nurses would come exactly as fast for five presses as for one. She was right on both counts.

Over the next three days she taught me the rest. Which nurse would bring a second pudding. How to work the bed so the leg stayed raised without the pillow sliding. That the doctors came at seven and asked how you felt, and that the true answer got you home faster than the brave one. I told her about the dare. She thought it was the funniest thing she had heard in weeks and said so, more than once.

Why she was there was the one subject we left alone. At eleven I believed that this was the decent thing, that a person in a hospital bed had the right to keep her reasons to herself, and I was a little pleased with myself for knowing it.

On the morning I went home, my mother brought a marker for the cast. Dana signed first, small, near the ankle: D., bed by the window. Then my mother wheeled me out to the car, and that was the last I saw of her.

The cast came off in February. The doctor cut it open with a little round saw that buzzed but, he promised, could not cut skin, and asked if I wanted to keep it. I did. I still have the piece with the ankle on it.

I have thought about that piece more than about the leg. For four days Dana answered every question I brought her. The one I kept back was the only one about her, and I kept it back, I think now, mostly because I was eleven and had decided that keeping it back made me considerate.

The other bed, the one by the window, belonged to a girl named Dana. She was fourteen and had been there, she told me, since before Halloween. It was the second week of December. In the 1890s, nearly every farmhouse in Brannock Hollow had a loom in it, and nearly every coverlet woven on those looms left the valley in the wagon of a single buyer, Amos Pruitt. Pruitt came through twice a year. He paid a dollar and a half for a coverlet that had taken a woman most of a month to weave, loaded it beside the others, and sold it in the city, the weavers later learned, for five or six.

Hester Keel learned it by accident. In the spring of 1897 her sister, who had married and moved to the city, mailed her a page torn from a department store catalog. On it, between a lamp and a set of dishes, was a coverlet in the Keel family's own pattern, a pine-tree border around a field of stars, priced at six dollars.

That summer Keel called a meeting in the Brannock Hollow church. Eleven women came. Her proposal was simple to state: they would stop selling to Pruitt, pool their coverlets, and ship them by rail to the store themselves. Pruitt, when he heard of it, told several husbands that a city store would never deal with a group of farm wives, and that the women would be begging him to come back by Christmas.

The store was willing, but it had conditions. It wanted coverlets of the same size, in colors that matched from one to the next, delivered by a set date. The Hollow's coverlets had never been alike; each family wove its own patterns, on looms of different widths, with wool dyed at home. Keel nailed a measuring stick to the wall of the church hall, and the members began dyeing their wool together, in one kettle, so that a blue from one house would match a blue from another.

Three of the original eleven left over the rule about patterns. The store would take only six, and a weaver whose grandmother's design was not among them had to choose between her pattern and the price.

The price was four dollars. By 1905 the cooperative had sixty-two members and sent a shipment every month, and Pruitt had stopped coming through the valley. The account book Keel kept for those years survives in the county historical society. In the back, on pages she seems to have kept for herself, she copied out by hand the patterns the store had refused, twenty-three of them, each with the name of the family that wove it.

A reef-building coral looks like a rock and behaves partly like a plant, and the reason lives inside it. Each coral is a colony of tiny animals called polyps, and in the tissue of most reef-building polyps live single-celled algae, packed by the millions into every square centimeter. The algae carry out photosynthesis and pass much of the sugar they make to the coral. In return, the coral gives them shelter, a place in the sunlight, and a supply of the carbon dioxide and nutrients its own body produces. For many corals, the algae provide most of their food. They also provide most of their color: coral tissue itself is nearly transparent.

This partnership works within a narrow band of temperature. When the water stays one or two degrees Celsius above the warmest it usually gets in summer, for several weeks, the arrangement breaks down. The stressed algae begin to produce harmful substances, and the coral expels them or loses them. With the algae gone, the clear tissue shows the white limestone skeleton beneath, and the coral is said to have bleached.

A bleached coral is not dead. It is starving. If the water cools within a few weeks, the few algae left in its tissue can multiply, or new ones can be taken in, and the coral slowly regains its color. If the heat lasts, the coral may die, and its skeleton is soon covered in a fuzz of other algae. Reefs that bleach once can recover over a decade or so, as surviving corals grow and young corals settle. Reefs that bleach again before that recovery is finished have a harder time.

That second problem is what concerns many reef scientists most. Large bleaching events were rarely recorded before the 1980s. Since then they have become more frequent as ocean temperatures have risen, and on some reefs the gap between them is now shorter than the time recovery seems to need.

The picture is not uniform. Some corals bleach more easily than others, and some reefs, cooled by currents or shaded by cloud, have fared better than their neighbors.
